title: Pyogenic granuloma
summary: A fast-growing, bright-red, friable lump that bleeds easily, often on a finger, lip or gum after minor injury or in pregnancy. Treat by curettage and cautery with histology, because amelanotic melanoma can look the same.

glance.think: A bright-red, shiny, easily bleeding lump that grew over a few weeks on a finger, lip, gum or face.
glance.engine: A reactive proliferation of small blood vessels, triggered by trauma, pregnancy or drugs (e.g. isotretinoin, some cancer drugs).
glance.backbone: Pressure for bleeding; refer for curettage and cautery and **always send for histology**; pregnancy lesions may resolve after birth.
glance.never_miss: Amelanotic nodular melanoma and SCC mimicking a pyogenic granuloma; recurrence if the base is not cauterised.

what: A common, benign, rapidly growing vascular tumour of skin and mucosa. The name is a misnomer: it is neither pyogenic nor a granuloma.
cause: Reactive proliferation of lobules of capillaries, often after minor trauma. Hormonal (pregnancy, the "granuloma gravidarum" on the gums) and **drug triggers**, which a pharmacist should know:

list: EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, erlotinib, gefitinib; around the nail folds)
A bright red, glistening, friable papule or polyp, 5–10 mm, developing over **weeks** (the 4-week series is in ). It often has a collarette of scale.
**Bleeds profusely with minor trauma.** Fingers, lips, gums, face, eyelid, and nail folds.
Clinical plus dermoscopy (red homogeneous areas, white "rail" lines, collarette).
**Histology is mandatory after removal, because amelanotic melanoma can look identical** (see , ).

differentials: **Amelanotic nodular melanoma** (the critical one; consider in any adult with a "PG" on a non-traumatised site, recurrence, or atypical vessels), SCC/keratoacanthoma, BCC, Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis (HIV), cherry angioma (older, stable), infantile haemangioma (infants), metastasis (kidney, thyroid), and periungual granulation tissue from an ingrown nail.

list: **Bleeding first aid:** firm pressure for 10–15 minutes; a non-adherent dressing.

**Refer for removal with histology.** Curettage and cautery (shave/curette plus base cautery) is the usual UK primary-care or dermatology approach. It is discussed at knowledge level in the [skin surgery](condition:skin-surgery-preop) notes.
Silver nitrate or cryotherapy alone gives no specimen and recurs more. Only use them where the diagnosis is not in doubt (e.g. a small pregnancy gum lesion, managed by a dentist).
**Drug-induced PG:** discuss with the prescribing specialist before stopping a cancer drug. Topical timolol or potent steroid are sometimes used by specialists for small periungual lesions.
Pregnancy PGs may regress after delivery; manage conservatively unless bleeding.

A **friable, bleeding vascular lesion** that would bleed during shave alone. **C&C removes it and seals the base**, and the curettings go for **histology** (amelanotic melanoma, SCC and Kaposi are the "must-not-miss" mimics; the [skin lumps](condition:dermatofibroma) notes see *Procedures at knowledge level*).

Alternatives: shave + cautery; excision for recurrent lesions (with closure, as course teaching described); silver nitrate or cryotherapy for very small lesions where the diagnosis is certain (no specimen).
**Posterior neck:** superficial procedures are safe. A deeper excision would need awareness of the spinal accessory nerve (see *Consent, complications and anatomical danger zones*).

red_flags: A rapidly growing red nodule in an adult, especially on the sole, nail unit or in someone over 50: send tissue for histology; refer on a **suspected cancer pathway** if atypical (amelanotic melanoma).
pearls: Recurrence (up to 15%) and satellite lesions happen. Return if it recurs, and do not assume it is benign.
On isotretinoin? PG-like granulation tissue at the nail folds is a known adverse effect. Report it (Yellow Card) and liaise with the prescriber.
